newsitem.title: USA: Turkey politics burden econ potential - US analysts.
newsitem.headline: Turkey politics burden econ potential - US analysts.

text.p: The turmoil that led Turkish Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan to step down Wednesday has hampered the country's efforts at economic stabilization and has made investment more risky, U.S. analysts said Wednesday.
After months of squabbles with the military establishment, Erbakan, the first Islamist to lead modern Turkey, resigned in a proposed power transfer to coalition ally Tansu Ciller.

U.S. analysts said Turkey, already wracked by high inflation and a hefty debt-service burden, needed to resolve its political turmoil in order to address its fiscal woes and achieve its growth potential.

"Turkey has a very serious issue on the fiscal front that requires definite action," said Amy Falls, head of sovereign research at Morgan Stanley. "It's not a stable equilibrium to run deficits at the rates that Turkey has been running."

Turkey's 1997 budget deficit is projected at 7.0 percent to 7.5 percent of gross domestic product, excluding any potential privatizations. That is down from close to 10 percent last year but still painfully high.
While Turkey made progress in trimming its deficit early this year, the country's efforts at fiscal discipline have stalled amid the recent turmoil, analysts said.

"It's continually surprising how resilient the economy is, but the trend on the fiscal side is negative," Falls said. "It's clear the economy would benefit from better, more focused macroeconomic policy."

Erbakan's resignation ended months of verbal sparring between the prime minister and the military, which views itself as the guardian of modern Turkish secularism. It accused Erbakan of failing to stem an surge in Islamist activism.

"The climate is unstable and there is a risk of volatility in the currency and the credit rating, but the fact is the risk is in the market," said Ali Naqvi, head of emerging market fixed income at Citibank Global Asset Management.

"There is some return to be had to be in there now, given the longer-term view that this is not an Algeria-like situation," Naqvi said, referring to Algeria's ongoing civil war between the secularist military and Islamist rebels.
In contrast, Morgan Stanley's Falls said Turkey's local debt markets did not offer compelling enough total returns to warrant the risk.
Turkey's political turmoil did not have a immediate impact on the country's credit ratings, which stood at Ba3 by Moody's Investors Service and single B by Standard & Poor's.
Marie Cavanaugh, S&P sovereign ratings analyst, said that Turkey's rating, the lowest of any sovereign nation that S&P rated, reflected potential for significant difficulties.
"It's our expectation that there will be continuing upward pressure on interest rates," Cavanaugh said. "We don't have the answer as to when the pressure becomes too extreme."

Cavanaugh said Turkey had improved its debt-servicing situation by lengthening the maturities of its domestic debt, and its "fairly strong external position" allowed for greater flexibility. But S&P would be watching the progress of these indicators.
"If those measures begin to erode in a significant fashion, there could be a possibility for some form of ratings adjustment," Cavanaugh said.
